doc.title: Panama Francis interviewed by Michael Woods, Los Angeles, California, September 1, 1995

title: Rhythm & Blues honor, the Rock 'n Roll label and its origins
summary: Honored in 1993 by the Rhythm & Blues Foundation, he was hurt that jazz musicians labeled him a Rock 'n Roll drummer; he traces R&B to the church and explains the origins of 'rock and roll' and 'funk'.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: But you have played with some of the great Rhythm & Blues artists.

Oh, well, I’ll tell you about that. Two years ago, in ‘93, they honored me, the Rhythm & Blues Foundation it’s called, out of Washington, D.C. They honored me for my contribution to Rhythm & Blues. But I was put down by the jazz musicians for playing Rhythm & Blues. Because that was the lowest — I mean they would record that music but they wasn’t too proud about it. And by me playing in the church when I was like nine years old, I used to play the Church of God, that was my gig on Sundays, I used to get fifty cents on Sundays for playing in church. I mean Rhythm & Blues came from the church.

I mean the only difference is the words were changed, but the music is the same. So that’s how I knew so much about Rhythm & Blues. And so I was called by the jazz musicians, I was called that Rock ‘n Roll drummer. It was a put down. Like we’d be in the bar at Jim and Andy’s and I’d walk in the door and they’d say “ohhh, here comes this Rock ‘n Roller.” Although they didn’t realize how much money I was making, but when they found out how much money I was making, they was knocking the door down to make them records. But anyhow, two years ago they honored me, they gave me fifteen thousand dollars and a plaque. And I went to make my acceptance speech and all I could say was “ladies and gentlemen“ and I bust out in tears, uncontrollable. Because I was hurt by the jazz musicians who knew me and knew that I worked in bands and heard me in jam sessions, and they went along with the white musicians who labeled me a Rock ‘n Roll musician. Because they never heard me play no jazz, because I was in Harlem all the © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -8-

time see, with the big bands. So they didn’t get a chance to hear me on 52nd Street. So they thought that this was all I could do, you know, that I was only able to play Rock ‘n Roll. And my friends and my so-called friends and brothers that knew different, never stood up and said well no man, he can play something else. I never got called for a big band date, I never got called for a jazz date. Very few jazz dates I did because of that. That was a label that was laid on me that wasn’t fair, because, I mean, I was able to play, you know, at the age of thirteen I was playing in bands. I wasn’t playing no Rhythm & Blues — I was playing in bands, playing arrangements and things. But I knew how to play this music, because I used to play in the church. Just like Rhythm & Blues became Rock ‘n Roll. I mean there was a disc jockey in Chicago named Al Benson that when he introduced his show, when he came on the air, he used to say “we’re gonna rock and we’re gonna roll this evening, children.” He sounded like a minister. And that’s where it came from. That’s where the Rock ‘n Roll came from. Alan Freed picked it up from Al Benson, ‘cause he thought that’s what the music was you know. It’s just like the word “funk.” That was a dirty word with black people. You told somebody to “funk” you’d be ready to fight. But the jazz critic heard the term being used by musicians, and they thought it was hip and it caught on. So they said “he sure plays funky, doesn’t he.” I remember the time you used that word that you’re liable to get your teeth knocked out of you. I mean that wasn’t a nice word.
